stories.title: Opening the oceans
stories.blurb: How did Iberian sailors, in a single generation, link Europe by sea to Africa, India, the Americas and the Pacific?

steps.date_note: landed at Mossel Bay on 3 February 1488 after rounding the Cape out of sight of land
steps.name: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
steps.what: Dias, sent by John II of Portugal with two caravels and a supply ship, was blown south past the tip of Africa and landed at Mossel Bay on the Indian Ocean side before his crew forced him to turn back.
steps.why: It proved that the Atlantic and Indian Oceans were connected and that a sea route to India around Africa was possible.

steps.name: Columbus sails from Palos
steps.what: Columbus left Palos with three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, and about 90 men, funded by Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon to reach Asia by sailing west.
steps.why: Castile backed a westward gamble because Portugal already controlled the route south around Africa.

steps.date_note: which Bahamian island was Guanahani is disputed
steps.name: Columbus reaches Guanahani
steps.what: After 33 days at sea from the Canary Islands, the fleet made landfall on an island the Lucayan people called Guanahani and Columbus named San Salvador.
steps.why: This first lasting contact joined the Americas to Europe and began the exchange of people, crops, animals and diseases between the hemispheres.

steps.name: Wreck of the Santa María and La Navidad
steps.what: The Santa María ran aground off northern Hispaniola on Christmas Day, and Columbus left 39 men in a fort built from its timbers, all of whom were dead when he returned in November 1493.
steps.why: La Navidad was the first European settlement attempt in the Americas, and its fate foreshadowed the violence of the colonial encounter.

steps.name: Treaty of Tordesillas
steps.what: Castile and Portugal divided the newly found lands outside Europe along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands, Portugal taking the east and Castile the west.
steps.why: Two kingdoms claimed the right to split the world's oceans between them, which shaped where each would explore and later why Brazil became Portuguese.

steps.name: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
steps.what: Da Gama, having sailed from Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships and picked up a pilot at Malindi, anchored near Calicut, the leading pepper port of the Malabar Coast ruled by the Zamorin.
steps.why: It opened the first all-sea route from Europe to Asia, letting Portugal bypass the Venetian and Middle Eastern middlemen of the spice trade.

steps.name: Cabral lands in Brazil
steps.what: Cabral's fleet of 13 ships, bound for India, swung far west into the Atlantic and sighted the coast of Brazil, which he claimed for Portugal before continuing to Calicut.
steps.why: Brazil fell on the Portuguese side of the Tordesillas line, giving Portugal its foothold in South America.

steps.name: Founding of the Casa de Contratación
steps.what: The Castilian crown set up a House of Trade in Seville to license ships, collect duties, train pilots and keep the master map of the routes to the Indies.
steps.why: Ocean exploration turned into a state-run business, and Seville became the monopoly port for all trade with Spanish America.

steps.name: Waldseemüller map names America
steps.what: Waldseemüller and his colleagues printed a large world map of 12 woodcut sheets that showed the new lands as a separate continent and labelled it America after Amerigo Vespucci.
steps.why: Printed maps spread the idea of a 'New World' distinct from Asia across Europe within a few years.

steps.date_note: the city fell on about 24 August 1511
steps.name: Capture of Malacca
steps.what: Albuquerque, with about 18 ships and some 1,000 Portuguese soldiers, took the sultanate of Malacca, the port that controlled the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.
steps.why: Portugal turned its sea route into a chain of armed trading forts reaching toward the spice islands and China.

steps.name: Balboa sights the Pacific
steps.what: Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama with Spanish soldiers and Indigenous guides and became the first European known to see the Pacific from the Americas, claiming it for Castile.
steps.why: It showed that a second ocean lay beyond the Americas, so a western route to Asia would need a passage through or around them.

steps.name: Magellan expedition sails
steps.what: Magellan, a Portuguese captain sailing for Charles I of Spain, left with five ships and about 270 men to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west.
steps.why: The aim was to prove the Moluccas lay on Castile's side of the Tordesillas line by reaching them westward.

steps.name: Passage of the Strait of Magellan
steps.what: After a mutiny and the loss of one ship, the fleet spent over five weeks threading the strait at the tip of South America; the San Antonio deserted and sailed home.
steps.why: Finding the strait opened the Pacific to European ships, though its width shocked the crews who then sailed for three months without landfall.

steps.name: Battle of Mactan
steps.what: Magellan, intervening in local politics after converting the ruler of Cebu, attacked the chief Lapulapu on Mactan and was killed with several of his men.
steps.why: The leader died halfway round the world, and the voyage had to be finished by others.

steps.name: Victoria completes the circumnavigation
steps.what: Elcano brought the Victoria home by way of the Indian Ocean and the Cape of Good Hope with 18 survivors and a cargo of cloves that more than paid for the voyage.
steps.why: The first circumnavigation joined all the oceans into one connected sea and showed how large the Earth really was.

stories.title: The Reformation
stories.blurb: How did one monk's protest split Western Christianity, and why could printing presses and princes make it stick?

steps.date_note: whether the theses were nailed to the church door is debated; the date is when Luther sent them to Archbishop Albert
steps.name: Ninety-five Theses
steps.what: Luther, a professor of theology, wrote 95 propositions attacking the sale of indulgences being preached by Johann Tetzel, and printed copies spread across Germany within weeks.
steps.why: A local academic dispute became a public controversy because printers in several cities reproduced it quickly.

steps.name: Leipzig Debate
steps.what: In a public disputation at Pleissenburg castle, Johann Eck pushed Luther into saying that popes and church councils could err.
steps.why: Luther's position moved from criticizing abuses to challenging the authority of the papacy itself.

steps.date_note: Luther appeared on 17 and 18 April; the Edict of Worms followed on 25 May
steps.name: Diet of Worms
steps.what: Before the young emperor Charles V and the imperial estates, Luther refused to recant his writings, and the Edict of Worms then declared him an outlaw.
steps.why: Luther survived only because his prince, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, protected him, showing that the movement depended on political backing.

steps.name: Luther at the Wartburg
steps.what: Hidden in the Wartburg under a false name, Luther translated the New Testament from Greek into German in about eleven weeks; it was printed in Wittenberg in September 1522.
steps.why: A cheap German Bible let ordinary readers judge scripture for themselves and helped shape a common written German.

steps.name: First Zurich Disputation
steps.what: Zurich's city council heard Zwingli defend 67 theses and ruled that he could go on preaching, putting the city on the path to its own reform.
steps.why: Reform began independently in the Swiss cities, run by town councils rather than princes, and soon diverged from Luther.

steps.name: Twelve Articles
steps.what: Peasant bands in Swabia met in Memmingen and adopted twelve demands, including the right to choose their pastors and an end to serfdom, citing scripture as justification.
steps.why: Printed in some 25,000 copies, the articles showed how the reformers' appeal to the Bible could be turned against lords.

steps.name: Battle of Frankenhausen
steps.what: Princely armies routed a peasant army led by the radical preacher Thomas Müntzer, killing thousands; Müntzer was captured and executed.
steps.why: The crushing of the Peasants' War, which Luther urged on, tied the Lutheran Reformation firmly to the princes.

steps.name: Marburg Colloquy
steps.what: Philip of Hesse brought Luther and Zwingli together to form a Protestant alliance, and they agreed on 14 of 15 points but not on the Lord's Supper.
steps.why: The Protestant movement split into Lutheran and Reformed branches that never reunited.

steps.name: Augsburg Confession
steps.what: Lutheran princes and cities read a statement of faith drafted by Melanchthon before Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg; the emperor rejected it.
steps.why: Lutheranism now had a defined creed, and its princes soon formed the Schmalkaldic League to defend it.

steps.name: Second War of Kappel
steps.what: Catholic Swiss cantons defeated Zurich's forces at Kappel, and Zwingli, serving as chaplain, was killed on the field.
steps.why: The Swiss Confederation settled into a patchwork of Catholic and Reformed cantons, a pattern repeated across Europe.

steps.name: Münster rebellion
steps.what: Radical Anabaptists took over the city of Münster and declared a new Jerusalem with shared property and polygamy until the besieging bishop's troops stormed it.
steps.why: The episode frightened Catholic and Protestant rulers alike and led to fierce persecution of Anabaptists.

steps.name: Act of Supremacy
steps.what: After the pope refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Henry VIII had Parliament declare him Supreme Head of the Church of England.
steps.why: England broke with Rome for dynastic and political reasons, showing that kings could use the Reformation to take control of their churches.

steps.name: Calvin returns to Geneva
steps.what: Recalled after an earlier expulsion, Calvin persuaded the city to adopt Ecclesiastical Ordinances creating a consistory of pastors and elders to supervise morals.
steps.why: Geneva became the training centre of a Reformed Protestantism that spread to France, Scotland, the Netherlands and later New England.

steps.name: Council of Trent
steps.what: The Catholic Church opened a general council that over 18 years restated its doctrines against the Protestants and ordered reforms such as seminaries for training priests.
steps.why: The Catholic answer to the Reformation fixed the doctrinal lines and ended hopes of reunion.

steps.name: Battle of Mühlberg
who: John Frederick I, Elector of Saxony
steps.what: Charles V defeated the Schmalkaldic League on the Elbe and captured the Lutheran Elector John Frederick of Saxony.
steps.why: Even a total military victory could not restore religious unity, as renewed Protestant resistance soon showed.

steps.name: Peace of Augsburg
steps.what: The imperial diet allowed each prince of the Empire to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his territory, a rule later summarized as cuius regio, eius religio.
steps.why: The split in Western Christianity was made legal and permanent, though Calvinists were left out, a gap that fed later wars.

stories.title: The Mughal empire
stories.blurb: How did a Central Asian prince's dynasty come to rule most of India, and why had it overstretched by 1707?

steps.name: First Battle of Panipat
steps.what: Babur, a Timurid prince from Kabul, used field guns and mounted archers to defeat the much larger army of Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, who died on the field.
steps.why: The victory gave Babur Delhi and Agra and founded the Mughal dynasty.

steps.name: Battle of Kannauj
steps.what: The Afghan leader Sher Shah Suri defeated Babur's son Humayun, who fled to Persia; Sher Shah then reorganized revenue collection and issued the silver rupiya.
steps.why: The Mughals nearly vanished after one generation, and their later administration borrowed heavily from Sher Shah's reforms.

steps.name: Second Battle of Panipat
steps.what: Months after Humayun's return and death, the forces of the 13-year-old Akbar and his regent Bairam Khan defeated Hemu, who was struck by an arrow and captured.
steps.why: The Mughals secured north India for good and Akbar's long reign began.

steps.name: Building of Fatehpur Sikri
steps.what: Akbar built a new red sandstone capital at Sikri, near the shrine of the Sufi Salim Chishti, and held court there until about 1585.
steps.why: The city displayed a blended Persian, Central Asian and Indian style that matched Akbar's effort to rule a diverse empire.

steps.name: Ibadat Khana debates
steps.what: Akbar built a House of Worship where Sunni and Shia scholars, and later Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit priests from Goa, debated religion before him.
steps.why: The debates fed Akbar's policy of tolerance, including his 1564 abolition of the jizya tax on non-Muslims.

steps.name: Ain-i-Akbari
steps.what: Akbar's minister Abu'l-Fazl compiled a detailed record of the empire, listing provinces, crop yields, prices, revenue rates and the ranks of the mansabdar officials.
steps.why: It documents the revenue machine, based on measured land and cash taxes, that paid for the Mughal army and court.

steps.name: Battle of Swally
steps.what: Four English East India Company ships under Thomas Best beat off a Portuguese fleet off Surat, and the Mughal authorities then allowed the English to open a trading post in the city.
steps.why: Surat, the empire's chief port, became the English company's first base in India.

steps.date_note: Roe reached Ajmer in December 1615 or January 1616 and stayed at court until 1619
steps.name: Thomas Roe at the court of Jahangir
steps.what: James I's ambassador spent three years following Jahangir's court and won permission for English trade, though not the formal treaty he wanted.
steps.why: The English came as petitioners to one of the richest states in the world, a reversal of the later balance of power.

steps.name: Building of the Taj Mahal
steps.what: Shah Jahan began a white marble tomb on the Yamuna for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631; the mausoleum was finished around 1643 and the whole complex around 1653.
steps.why: The Taj shows the wealth and artistic peak of the empire under Shah Jahan.

steps.name: Building of the Red Fort
steps.what: Shah Jahan moved the capital from Agra to a new walled city at Delhi, Shahjahanabad, built around the Red Fort palace and the Chandni Chowk market street.
steps.why: The new capital, with its markets and mosques, became the centre of Mughal government and of a large urban economy.

steps.name: Battle of Samugarh
steps.what: In the war of succession among Shah Jahan's sons, Aurangzeb defeated his elder brother Dara Shikoh, then imprisoned his father in Agra fort until his death in 1666.
steps.why: Aurangzeb, a stricter Sunni ruler, took the throne and set the course of the empire's last great expansion.

steps.name: Sack of Surat
steps.what: The Maratha leader Shivaji plundered the rich Mughal port of Surat for several days, while the English and Dutch factories defended themselves.
steps.why: Maratha power in the western Deccan grew into the most serious challenge to Mughal rule.

steps.name: Siege of Golconda
steps.what: Aurangzeb, campaigning in the Deccan since 1681, took the diamond-trading fortress of Golconda after eight months, a year after annexing Bijapur.
steps.why: The empire reached its greatest size, but the long Deccan wars drained its treasury and nobility.

steps.name: Death of Aurangzeb
steps.what: Aurangzeb died aged 88 in camp in the Deccan after more than 25 years of war against the Marathas, which he had not won.
steps.why: Succession wars followed, and within decades provincial governors and the Marathas held real power while emperors in Delhi became figureheads.

stories.title: The Thirty Years' War
stories.blurb: How did a Bohemian revolt grow into a war that drew in most of Europe and killed millions in the German lands?

steps.name: Defenestration of Prague
steps.what: Protestant Bohemian nobles threw two Catholic imperial governors and their secretary out of a window of Prague Castle; all three survived the fall.
steps.why: The act launched a Bohemian revolt against the Habsburgs that became the first phase of the war.

steps.name: Battle of White Mountain
steps.what: Imperial and Catholic League troops under Tilly routed the Bohemian army in about two hours, and the rebels' elected king, Frederick V of the Palatinate, fled.
steps.why: Bohemia was forced back under Habsburg and Catholic rule, but the war spread to Frederick's lands in the Rhineland.

steps.name: Old Town Square execution
steps.what: Twenty-seven leaders of the Bohemian revolt were executed in Prague's main square, and the heads of twelve were displayed on the Old Town Bridge Tower.
steps.why: Mass confiscations of land and forced conversions followed, which drove many Protestants into exile.

steps.name: Battle of Lutter
steps.what: Tilly defeated the army of Christian IV of Denmark, who had entered the war to protect the Protestant states of northern Germany.
steps.why: The Danish intervention failed, leaving the emperor dominant in the north.

steps.name: Siege of Stralsund
steps.what: Wallenstein's imperial army besieged the Baltic port of Stralsund, which held out with Danish and Swedish help until he gave up.
steps.why: Habsburg ambitions on the Baltic coast alarmed Sweden and drew it toward the war.

steps.name: Edict of Restitution
steps.what: Ferdinand II ordered the return to the Catholic Church of all church lands taken by Protestants since 1552.
steps.why: The edict alarmed even Protestant princes who had stayed loyal and made a negotiated peace harder.

steps.name: Swedish landing in Pomerania
steps.what: Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed on the island of Usedom with about 13,000 men, later backed by French subsidies.
steps.why: The war turned into an international contest in which Catholic France paid a Lutheran king to fight the Habsburgs.
steps.wikipedia: Swedish intervention in the Thirty Years' War

steps.name: Sack of Magdeburg
steps.what: Imperial troops stormed the Protestant city, and in the massacre and fire that followed about 20,000 of its 25,000 inhabitants died.
steps.why: Magdeburg became a byword for the war's cruelty toward civilians and pushed hesitant Protestant states toward Sweden.

steps.name: Battle of Breitenfeld
who: John George I, Elector of Saxony
steps.what: The Swedish and Saxon army destroyed Tilly's veteran force using flexible lines of musketeers and light field guns.
steps.why: It was the first major Protestant victory of the war and opened southern Germany to Swedish armies.

steps.name: Battle of Lützen
steps.what: The Swedes drove Wallenstein from the field in fog, but Gustavus Adolphus and the imperial general Pappenheim were both killed.
steps.why: Sweden lost its king and leader, and the war dragged on without a decisive winner.

steps.name: Oberammergau plague vow
steps.what: After plague spread by the war reached their Bavarian village, the people of Oberammergau vowed to stage a play of Christ's Passion every ten years, first performing it in 1634.
steps.why: Disease and hunger that followed the armies killed far more people than battles did, and the vow is still kept today.

steps.name: Assassination of Wallenstein
steps.what: Wallenstein, the military contractor who had raised huge armies for the emperor, was killed by his own officers after Ferdinand II suspected him of secret talks with the enemy.
steps.why: His career shows how the war was run by private enterprisers who fed their troops by taxing and plundering the land.

steps.name: Battle of Nördlingen
steps.what: A combined Spanish and imperial army crushed the Swedish and German Protestant forces in southern Germany.
steps.why: The defeat pushed France to enter the war openly in 1635, turning it into a Bourbon-Habsburg struggle that lasted another 13 years.

steps.name: Peace of Westphalia
steps.what: Treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück ended the war, recognized Calvinism alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism, gave Sweden and France territory and confirmed the independence of the Dutch Republic and Switzerland.
steps.why: The settlement closed Europe's wars of religion in the Empire after a conflict estimated to have killed 4.5 to 8 million people, mostly through disease and famine.

stories.title: The Dutch golden age
stories.region: Netherlands and the Dutch seaborne empire
stories.blurb: How did a small, rebellious republic become the center of world trade and finance in the seventeenth century?

steps.name: Fall of Antwerp
steps.what: Spanish forces under Parma took Antwerp after a 14-month siege; Protestants were given time to leave, and the Dutch rebels closed the Scheldt to shipping.
steps.why: Tens of thousands of merchants and craftsmen moved north, carrying capital and skills to Amsterdam.

steps.name: First Dutch voyage reaches Banten
steps.what: Four ships under Cornelis de Houtman reached the pepper port of Banten on Java after 14 months, and returned in 1597 with only 87 of 249 men alive.
steps.why: The voyage barely paid, but it proved Dutch ships could reach the spice islands, setting off a rush of rival companies.
steps.wikipedia: First Dutch Expedition to the East Indies

steps.name: Founding of the Dutch East India Company
steps.what: The States General merged the competing companies into the United East India Company (VOC), with a monopoly on Dutch trade east of the Cape and the right to wage war and make treaties.
steps.why: The VOC sold shares to the public that could be traded, creating a new kind of permanent, armed joint-stock company.

steps.name: Founding of the Bank of Amsterdam
steps.what: The city founded the Amsterdamsche Wisselbank, where merchants could deposit coins of uncertain quality and pay each other by transfer in reliable bank money.
steps.why: Stable money and cheap credit made Amsterdam the clearing house of European trade.

steps.name: Amsterdam Exchange building opens
steps.what: A purpose-built exchange designed by Hendrick de Keyser opened on the Rokin, where VOC shares and commodities were traded at fixed hours.
steps.why: Regular trading in company shares, including forward contracts, made Amsterdam home to the first modern stock market.

steps.name: Founding of Batavia
steps.what: Governor-General Coen destroyed the town of Jayakarta and built Batavia on its ruins as the VOC's headquarters in Asia.
steps.why: Batavia became the hub of a Dutch trading network stretching from Persia to Japan, governed by force.

steps.name: Amboyna massacre
steps.what: VOC officials on Ambon tortured and executed ten Englishmen, nine Japanese and one Portuguese accused of plotting to seize the fort.
steps.why: The English largely withdrew from the spice islands, leaving the Dutch in control of cloves and nutmeg.

steps.name: Purchase of Manhattan
steps.what: Peter Minuit of the Dutch West India Company bought Manhattan from the Lenape for goods valued at 60 guilders, and the settlement of New Amsterdam grew at its southern tip.
steps.why: The Dutch built an Atlantic trading network for furs, sugar and enslaved people alongside their Asian one.

steps.name: Collapse of tulip mania
steps.what: Prices for rare tulip bulbs, traded in taverns through contracts for future delivery, collapsed in early February 1637 when buyers stopped appearing at an auction in Haarlem.
steps.why: The episode, smaller than its legend, shows how much wealth and speculative trading the Dutch economy generated.

steps.name: Dutch moved to Dejima
steps.what: The Tokugawa shogunate ordered the VOC to move its trading post from Hirado to Dejima, a small artificial island in Nagasaki harbor.
steps.why: For two centuries the Dutch were the only Europeans allowed to trade with Japan, earning silver and copper for the Asian trade.

steps.name: The Night Watch
steps.what: Rembrandt completed a large group portrait of an Amsterdam civic militia company commanded by Frans Banninck Cocq, commissioned for their meeting hall.
steps.why: Wealthy citizens, not just princes and churches, paid for art, and Dutch painting flourished on an open market.

steps.name: Founding of Cape Town
steps.what: Jan van Riebeeck landed with about 90 VOC employees to build a fort and gardens to supply fresh food to ships sailing between Europe and Asia.
steps.why: A supply station became a settler colony that pushed onto Khoekhoe land and imported enslaved workers.

steps.name: Raid on the Medway
steps.what: A Dutch fleet under De Ruyter sailed up the Thames estuary and the Medway, burned English warships at anchor and towed away the flagship Royal Charles.
steps.why: Dutch naval power peaked, forcing England to accept a favourable peace at Breda.

steps.name: Rampjaar and the lynching of the De Witt brothers
steps.what: In the 'disaster year' when France, England, Münster and Cologne invaded at once, a mob in The Hague killed the Grand Pensionary Johan de Witt and his brother Cornelis, and William III of Orange took power.
steps.why: The Republic survived by flooding the land, but 1672 is usually taken as the end of its golden age.

stories.title: Japan unified and closed
stories.blurb: How did three warlords end a century of civil war in Japan, and why did their successors close the country to most foreigners?

steps.name: Battle of Okehazama
steps.what: Oda Nobunaga, with perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 men, surprised the far larger army of Imagawa Yoshimoto in a rainstorm and killed him.
steps.why: A minor lord from Owari became a major contender in the wars of the Sengoku period.

steps.name: Nobunaga enters Kyoto
steps.what: Nobunaga marched on the capital and installed Ashikaga Yoshiaki as shogun, whom he later drove out in 1573.
steps.why: Control of Kyoto gave Nobunaga the prestige to claim to act for the whole realm.

steps.name: Battle of Nagashino
steps.what: Behind wooden palisades, the arquebusiers of Nobunaga and Ieyasu shattered the charges of Takeda Katsuyori's cavalry.
steps.why: Firearms, introduced by Portuguese traders in 1543, had become decisive in Japanese warfare.

steps.name: Building of Azuchi Castle
steps.what: Nobunaga built a castle with a seven-storey keep on Lake Biwa and declared the town below a free market, open to merchants without guild fees.
steps.why: Unifiers paired military force with policies that encouraged commerce in their castle towns.

steps.name: Honnō-ji Incident
steps.what: Nobunaga's general Akechi Mitsuhide attacked him at the Honnō-ji temple, where Nobunaga died; Hideyoshi defeated Mitsuhide 11 days later.
steps.why: Leadership of the unification passed to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, a commander of humble birth.

steps.name: Hideyoshi's sword hunt
steps.what: Hideyoshi ordered farmers to hand over swords and guns, alongside land surveys that recorded the yield of every field and the household responsible for it.
steps.why: The measures fixed a line between armed samurai and taxpaying farmers that structured Japanese society for nearly three centuries.

steps.name: Siege of Odawara
steps.what: Hideyoshi surrounded the Hōjō clan's castle with a huge army until it surrendered, and gave the Hōjō lands in the Kantō to Ieyasu.
steps.why: The last major independent warlord fell, completing the political unification of Japan.

steps.name: Siege of Busanjin
steps.what: Japanese troops landed at Busan and took the fortress in a day, beginning an invasion of Korea by about 150,000 men aiming eventually at Ming China.
steps.why: Hideyoshi turned the armies of a unified Japan outward, in a war that devastated Korea.

steps.name: Battle of Hansan Island
steps.what: Admiral Yi Sun-sin lured a Japanese fleet into open water and destroyed most of its ships.
steps.why: Korean control of the sea cut Japanese supply lines, and with Ming intervention the invasion stalled; Japan withdrew after Hideyoshi's death in 1598.

steps.name: Battle of Sekigahara
steps.what: Ieyasu's eastern army defeated the western coalition led by Ishida Mitsunari after Kobayakawa Hideaki switched sides mid-battle.
steps.why: Ieyasu became the unchallenged power in Japan.

steps.name: Tokugawa shogunate founded
steps.what: The emperor appointed Ieyasu shogun, and he governed from his castle town of Edo, which grew into one of the world's largest cities.
steps.why: The Tokugawa regime lasted until 1868, giving Japan more than 250 years without major war.

steps.name: Siege of Osaka
steps.what: In winter and summer campaigns Ieyasu besieged and burned Osaka Castle; Hideyoshi's son Hideyori and his mother died by suicide.
steps.why: The destruction of the Toyotomi removed the last rival to Tokugawa rule.

steps.name: Sankin-kōtai made compulsory
steps.what: Shogun Iemitsu required the daimyo to spend alternate years in Edo and to leave their wives and heirs there permanently.
steps.why: The costly processions kept lords in check and built up the roads, inns and markets that linked the country.

steps.name: Shimabara Rebellion
steps.what: Overtaxed peasants, many of them Christian, rose under the teenage Amakusa Shirō and held Hara Castle until a shogunate army of over 100,000 stormed it and killed the defenders.
steps.why: The shogunate blamed Christianity and its Portuguese carriers, hardening its policy against foreign influence.

steps.name: Expulsion of the Portuguese
steps.what: The last of a series of edicts banned Portuguese ships from Japan, completing measures that already forbade Japanese to travel abroad.
steps.why: Japan's foreign contact was limited to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki and to Korea, the Ryukyus and the Ainu through intermediaries.

stories.title: The Atlantic slave trade
stories.blurb: How did sugar drive the forced migration of millions of Africans across the Atlantic, and how did Britain come to ban the trade?

steps.name: First licence for direct shipment from Africa
steps.what: Charles I of Spain granted a licence to ship 4,000 enslaved Africans directly from Africa to the Spanish Indies; such licences later became the asiento contracts.
steps.why: The Spanish crown turned the supply of enslaved labour to its colonies into a regulated, taxed business.

steps.name: Founding of Salvador da Bahia
steps.what: Tomé de Sousa founded Salvador as the capital of Portuguese Brazil, at the centre of the sugar-growing lands around the Bay of All Saints.
steps.why: Brazil's sugar mills, first worked by Indigenous people and then by enslaved Africans, made it the world's leading sugar producer by 1600.

steps.name: Founding of Luanda
steps.what: Paulo Dias de Novais founded Luanda on the coast of Angola as a Portuguese base.
steps.why: West Central Africa, through Luanda and nearby ports, became the largest single source of people taken across the Atlantic.

steps.name: Dutch Brazil
steps.what: The Dutch West India Company seized Olinda and Recife in Pernambuco and ran the sugar colony until Portuguese colonists drove them out in 1654.
steps.why: The Dutch learned sugar production and the slave trade in Brazil and carried that knowledge to the Caribbean.

steps.name: Dutch capture of Elmina
steps.what: The Dutch West India Company took São Jorge da Mina, the fort the Portuguese had built on the Gold Coast in 1482.
steps.why: Forts on the West African coast, first built for gold, became holding places for enslaved captives awaiting ships.

steps.date_note: c.; the shift to sugar happened during the 1640s
steps.name: Barbados turns to sugar
steps.what: English planters on Barbados switched from tobacco and cotton to sugar, using methods learned from Dutch Brazil, and replaced indentured servants with enslaved Africans.
steps.why: By the 1660s Barbados was England's richest colony and the model for the plantation system across the Caribbean.

steps.name: Royal African Company chartered
steps.what: Charles II granted a new company headed by his brother James, Duke of York, a monopoly on English trade with West Africa; it branded captives with its initials.
steps.why: The company shipped more enslaved Africans than any other single British institution in the trade's history.

steps.name: Peace of Utrecht and the British asiento
steps.what: Among the treaties ending the War of the Spanish Succession, Spain granted Britain the asiento, the right to supply 4,800 enslaved Africans a year to Spanish America for 30 years.
steps.why: European powers treated the slave trade as a prize of war, and the contract passed to the South Sea Company.

steps.name: Dahomey conquers Ouidah
steps.what: King Agaja of Dahomey conquered the coastal kingdom of Hueda and its port of Ouidah.
steps.why: African states controlled the supply of captives on the coast, and Ouidah became one of the busiest slave ports in Africa.

steps.date_note: representative date; the trade peaked in the second half of the 18th century
steps.name: The Middle Passage
steps.what: Between 1501 and 1866 about 12.5 million Africans were put on ships for the Americas and about 10.7 million survived the crossing, which usually took one to two months.
steps.why: The crossing itself killed well over a million people and was the core of a trade built on sugar, tobacco, cotton and coffee.

steps.date_note: killings began on 29 November 1781 and continued over several days
steps.name: Zong massacre
steps.what: The crew of the Liverpool-owned slave ship Zong threw about 130 or more Africans overboard, and the owners then claimed insurance for them as lost cargo.
steps.why: When Olaudah Equiano told Granville Sharp, the 1783 insurance case became a rallying point for the abolition movement.

steps.name: Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade founded
steps.what: Twelve men, nine of them Quakers, met at a printing shop in George Yard and formed a committee to campaign against the slave trade.
steps.why: It began one of the first mass public campaigns, using petitions, boycotts of slave-grown sugar and printed evidence.
steps.wikipedia: Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade

steps.name: Diagram of the slave ship Brooks
steps.what: Abolitionists in Plymouth printed a plan of the Liverpool slave ship Brooks showing how hundreds of captives were packed below deck; thousands of copies circulated.
steps.why: The image made the Middle Passage visible to the public and became the movement's most famous print.

steps.name: Haitian Revolution begins
steps.what: Enslaved people in northern Saint-Domingue, the world's richest sugar colony with about half a million enslaved, rose up and burned plantations.
steps.why: The only successful large-scale slave revolt created the free state of Haiti in 1804 and shook every slave society in the Americas.

steps.name: Slave Trade Act 1807
steps.what: After two decades of campaigning led in Parliament by William Wilberforce, Britain banned the slave trade within its empire, with effect for ships from 1 May 1807.
steps.why: Britain, the leading slave-trading nation of the late 1700s, now used its navy against the trade, though slavery itself lasted in British colonies until 1834.

stories.title: The Qing conquest and High Qing
stories.blurb: How did Manchu invaders conquer Ming China and build the largest and richest empire in its history, and what strains showed by 1799?

steps.name: Fall of Beijing to Li Zicheng
steps.what: The rebel army of Li Zicheng entered Beijing and the last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, hanged himself on Coal Hill behind the palace.
steps.why: The Ming fell to internal rebellion driven by famine and fiscal collapse, opening the way for the Manchus.

steps.name: Battle of Shanhai Pass
steps.what: The Ming general Wu Sangui opened the eastern end of the Great Wall to the Manchu regent Dorgon, and their combined army defeated Li Zicheng.
steps.why: The Qing entered Beijing in June 1644 and claimed the Mandate of Heaven.

steps.name: Yangzhou massacre
steps.what: After the Ming loyalist Shi Kefa refused to surrender, Qing troops under Dodo took Yangzhou and killed a large part of its population over ten days.
steps.why: The massacre, followed by the order that all men shave their heads in the Manchu queue, showed the price of resistance in the south.

steps.name: Siege of Fort Zeelandia
steps.what: The Ming loyalist Koxinga crossed to Taiwan with a large fleet and forced the Dutch governor Frederick Coyett to surrender Fort Zeelandia after nine months.
steps.why: Koxinga's family made Taiwan a loyalist base and a maritime trading state outside Qing control.

steps.name: Revolt of the Three Feudatories
steps.what: When the young Kangxi Emperor moved to abolish their semi-independent fiefs in the south, Wu Sangui and two other Chinese generals rebelled; the Qing won after eight years.
steps.why: Kangxi's victory consolidated direct Qing rule over all of China proper.

steps.date_note: imperial kilns restored in the early 1680s
steps.name: Revival of the Jingdezhen imperial kilns
steps.what: After war damage, the imperial porcelain works at Jingdezhen were rebuilt under supervisors sent from court, and the town's thousands of kilns again produced for both palace and export.
steps.why: Porcelain, with silk and tea, brought silver from Europe and the Americas into China.

steps.name: Battle of Penghu
steps.what: The Qing admiral Shi Lang destroyed the Zheng fleet in the Penghu islands, and the Zheng regime on Taiwan surrendered soon after.
steps.why: Taiwan became part of the Qing empire, and the coast was reopened to trade in 1684.

steps.name: Treaty of Nerchinsk
steps.what: Qing and Russian envoys, with Jesuits translating in Latin, fixed the border along the Argun River and the Stanovoy mountains and allowed trade.
steps.why: The first treaty between China and a European power stopped Russia's advance into the Amur valley and freed Kangxi to turn on the Dzungars.

steps.name: Kangxi Dictionary
steps.what: Scholars commissioned by the emperor completed a dictionary of about 47,000 characters, which remained the standard reference for two centuries.
steps.why: The Manchu rulers won over Chinese scholar elites by sponsoring large works of classical learning.

steps.name: Dzungar genocide
steps.what: After the Dzungar leader Amursana rebelled, the Qianlong Emperor ordered the Dzungars destroyed; war, killings and smallpox wiped out most of a population of several hundred thousand.
steps.why: The last great steppe empire was eliminated, and the conquered lands became Xinjiang, doubling the empire's area.

steps.name: Canton System
steps.what: Qianlong restricted European seaborne trade to Guangzhou, where foreigners had to deal only through licensed merchants of the Cohong.
steps.why: The Qing kept Western trade under tight control while the tea trade with Britain grew enormously.

steps.name: Compilation of the Siku Quanshu
steps.what: Qianlong had hundreds of scholars copy about 3,500 works into a collection of some 36,000 volumes, while books judged hostile to the Manchus were destroyed.
steps.why: The project shows both the scale of High Qing patronage and its censorship.

steps.name: Macartney Embassy received by Qianlong
steps.what: Lord Macartney presented George III's letter to the 82-year-old emperor at his summer residence; Qianlong refused requests for wider trade and a resident ambassador.
steps.why: The confident refusal reflected Qing power, but Britain's growing demand for trade would return with force in the Opium War.

steps.name: White Lotus Rebellion
steps.what: Followers of the White Lotus sect in the poor hill country where Hubei, Sichuan and Shaanxi meet rose against taxes and officials and held out for nine years.
steps.why: Rapid population growth to around 300 million and corrupt government were straining the empire.

steps.name: Death of Qianlong and fall of Heshen
steps.what: Days after the retired Qianlong Emperor died, his son the Jiaqing Emperor arrested Qianlong's favourite minister Heshen, ordered him to commit suicide and seized a fortune said to rival years of state revenue.
steps.why: The scandal exposed the corruption that had grown at the top during the High Qing.
